section.title: To the Church in Smyrna
section.sectionRationale: The second of the seven letters, and the shortest, containing no rebuke at all, unlike the letter just before it. A poor, slandered congregation on the edge of imprisonment and death is addressed by the very one who himself died and returned to life, and is comforted rather than corrected.
section.thesis: To a poor, slandered church facing imminent imprisonment and testing, the First and the Last, who died and returned to life, speaks no word of complaint, only comfort: do not fear, be faithful even to death, and receive the crown of life, safe forever from the second death.
section.frameNote: Two units: Christ's self-description as the one who died and lives, and his commendation of Smyrna's true riches amid affliction and slander (8-9); his charge not to fear coming imprisonment and testing, with the promise of the crown of life and safety from the second death (10-11).

verses.text: To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life.

I know your affliction and your {{ptocheia|poverty}}, though you are rich! And I am aware of the slander of those who falsely claim to be Jews, but are in fact a {{synagoge_satana|synagogue of Satan}}.

Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will suffer tribulation for ten days. Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you {{stephanos_zoes|the crown of life}}.
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who overcomes will not be harmed by {{thanatos_deuteros|the second death}}.

ptocheia.gloss: Poverty, often meaning destitution rather than modest means, likely worsened by economic exclusion under persecution. Christ immediately reframes it: 'though you are rich,' true wealth measured by fidelity to him rather than by coin.

synagoge_satana.gloss: Synagogue of Satan. A severe phrase for a local hostile faction whose slander aligned it, in this instance, with the accuser rather than with God's true Israel; it names a specific opposition in Smyrna, not Jewish people in general.

stephanos_zoes.gloss: The crown of life, the victor's wreath awarded at the games, here promised for faithfulness even to death. The same exact phrase appears in James 1:12, given to those who love the Lord and endure trial.

thanatos_deuteros.gloss: The second death, a phrase unique to Revelation, appearing again in 20:6, 20:14, and 21:8, naming final, eternal separation from God after the resurrection and judgment. The overcomer in Smyrna, though facing physical death, is promised complete safety from this second, ultimate death.

basic.context: Smyrna's letter is short and contains no rebuke at all, the only other exception being Philadelphia's letter later. Christ knows this congregation's affliction, poverty, and the slander of a hostile local group, and tells them plainly that some of them are about to be imprisoned and tested, with suffering lasting 'ten days.' Rather than a complaint, he offers only comfort: do not fear, be faithful even to death, and receive the crown of life.
basic.hermeneutics: The letter is read straightforwardly as addressed to a real, persecuted church in the city of Smyrna, later home to the martyr Polycarp. The 'ten days' is widely read as a short, divinely limited period of testing rather than a literal count to calculate, and 'synagogue of Satan' is read as naming a specific hostile local group, not a verdict on Jewish people as a whole.
basic.originalLanguages: Christ knows their ptocheia, real poverty, yet declares them rich. He names the slander of a synagoge tou Satana, a synagogue of Satan, a local hostile faction. The reward for enduring even to death is the stephanos tes zoes, the crown of life, and the promise of complete safety from ho deuteros thanatos, the second death.
basic.typology: The crown of life echoes the ancient world's victor's wreath and finds its full New Testament parallel in James 1:12. The 'ten days' recalls Daniel's ten-day test in Daniel 1:12-14, a brief, bounded trial that ends in vindication. Christ's title, 'who died and returned to life,' answers and reverses the fear of death itself.
basic.christ: Christ introduces himself here as the First and the Last, who died and returned to life, the very self-description he used to comfort John in chapter 1. To a church facing death, he speaks first as one who has already been through death and come out the other side alive forever, making his call to be 'faithful even unto death' credible rather than merely demanding.
basic.god: God is shown here setting real limits on suffering, 'ten days,' not open-ended, and standing sovereign even over the devil's actions, who is 'about to throw some of you into prison.' The full weight of persecution's fear is met with the full weight of divine sovereignty and promised reward.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 1:12-14 gives a ten-day test that ends in vindication. James 1:12 promises the crown of life to those who endure trial. Romans 2:28-29 clarifies who is truly a Jew before God. Revelation 20:14 and 21:8 describe the second death as the lake of fire, from which overcomers are safe.
basic.oneStory: To the poorest, most afflicted of the seven churches, Christ offers no rebuke, only the comfort of one who has already died and lives forever. Their trial is bounded, their poverty conceals true riches, and their faithfulness even to death leads to a crown of life and complete safety from the only death that finally matters, the whole Bible's promise that God vindicates his suffering people made concrete for one small, persecuted congregation.

context.literary:
The letters to the seven churches share one frame: a command to write, a title of Christ lifted from the vision of Revelation 1, the words 'I know', a verdict, a summons, a promise to the one who overcomes, and the call to hear. Smyrna's letter keeps every part of that frame and fills most of it with consolation. Only Smyrna and Philadelphia receive no rebuke, and the two are linked further by the same phrase, 'synagogue of Satan,' Revelation 2:9 and 3:9. They are also the two churches whose outward circumstances are the hardest, as if the Lord measured a congregation by the cost of its loyalty rather than by its comfort.

The letter is built on three reversals. The first sits in verse 9, where poverty and riches are set against each other in a single breath, 'your poverty, though you are rich.' The second sits in verse 8 and verse 10, where the one who 'died and returned to life' commands a church to be faithful 'unto death.' The third sits in verse 11, where an overcomer who may die in the first sense is promised that the second death will not touch him. Each reversal tells the church that the visible account is not the true account.

The title in verse 8 is not chosen at random. 'The First and the Last' is the divine title John heard in Revelation 1:17, and 'who died and returned to life' picks up the very next words of that scene, 'I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever,' Revelation 1:18. Everything the letter asks, the speaker has already done.

The imperatives gather in verse 10: do not fear, be faithful, and a promise beside them. Fear is addressed before faithfulness, because the Lord knows that fear is what would break the second.
context.historical:
Smyrna, on the Aegean coast of Asia, was one of the great harbour cities of the province and proud of it. It was proud of its beauty and had been an early and eager friend of Rome and was among the first cities in the region to build a temple to the goddess Roma. Faith in Christ in such a place was not merely a private belief; it set believers against the civic habit of honouring the empire's divine claims.

The affliction and poverty of verse 9 fit that pressure. Trade in a harbour city ran through guilds, markets and festivals tied to the gods, and a Christian who stepped away from them could lose his livelihood. Poverty here is the cost of a choice, not a misfortune.

The slander is traced to people who 'falsely claim to be Jews.' Smyrna had a Jewish community, and the early Christians had begun as a movement within the synagogue, so the quarrel was a family quarrel with heavy stakes. Informing against believers to the authorities was a ready way to turn a religious dispute into a legal danger, and the letter's mention of prison in verse 10 suggests that this is how it may have worked. The Lord does not condemn a people; He names a particular opposition that has aligned itself with the accuser.

Smyrna later gave the church one of its best known martyrs. Polycarp, its bishop, was put to death in the middle of the second century, and the account of his death remembers the faithfulness this letter asks for. That is later history, not a fulfilment of the letter's prediction, but it shows that 'be faithful even unto death' was a real calling in this city and not a figure of speech.
context.canonical:
The promise of a crown reaches back through the whole biblical story of reward. In Proverbs wisdom bestows 'a garland of grace' on her follower, Proverbs 4:9, and in the New Testament the crown is the image of final reward for those who endure: the 'crown of life' in James 1:12, the 'crown of righteousness' that Paul expects, 2 Timothy 4:8, and the 'crown of glory that will never fade away' that the Chief Shepherd gives, 1 Peter 5:4. Revelation's own twenty four elders wear crowns, Revelation 4:4, and cast them before the throne in verse 10 of the same chapter, which shows what the crown is for.

The ten days of verse 10 echo Daniel 1:12 to 14, where a short, defined test ends in vindication. The note of a limit is the point. Suffering that comes 'for ten days' is suffering the Lord has measured.

The second death, a phrase found only in Revelation, is explained as the lake of fire in Revelation 20:14 and 21:8. Those who have a share in the first resurrection are promised that the second death 'has no power over them,' Revelation 20:6, which is the promise of Smyrna's verse 11 taken to its end.

The contrast of poverty and riches is carried through the New Testament as a standing paradox of the kingdom. Paul writes that the apostles are 'poor, yet making many rich,' 2 Corinthians 6:10, and Jesus says in the same book that Laodicea, which says 'I am rich,' is in truth poor, Revelation 3:17. Smyrna and Laodicea are mirror images, one poor and rich, the other rich and poor.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Lord who speaks here intends the church to take two things from the letter and to hold them together. First, nothing in their suffering is out of His sight. 'I know' opens the verdict, and what He knows is named plainly: affliction, poverty, slander. Persecuted believers are tempted to think that heaven has not noticed, and the letter answers that it has.

Second, He intends them to take courage rather than only comfort. 'Do not fear' is not a soothing phrase to be left floating; it carries a reason, and the reason is the speaker Himself. He is the First and the Last, which means He was before their trial and will be after it, and He is the one who died and returned to life, which means He has already walked the road He is asking them to walk. The command to be faithful until death is therefore not a stern demand from a safe distance but an invitation to follow.

He also means to set the true measure of a church. By the world's accounts Smyrna was weak and poor. By His account it was rich. A congregation reading this letter would be taught to judge its own health by faithfulness under pressure, not by size, resources or reputation.

Finally the letter is meant to prepare the church for what is coming. 'About to suffer' tells them that the worst has not yet happened. A warning given before the storm is a mercy, because it takes away the shock that would otherwise be mistaken for abandonment.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The letter describes the particular situation of one congregation: a coming imprisonment, a ten day period of testing, a hostile faction in the city. These are not forecasts for every church, and a reader should not expect to find the same details repeated. What carries over is the pattern of the Lord's care, not the pattern of the circumstances.

The commands are prescriptive and are meant to be taken at full weight: do not fear, be faithful, hear what the Spirit says. 'Even unto death' sets the limit of loyalty, not a call to seek martyrdom. The text asks for faithfulness when death comes, not for a pursuit of it.

Care is needed with the phrase 'synagogue of Satan.' It describes a specific group in a specific city that slandered Christians. It does not give later readers licence to speak of Jewish people as a whole in such terms, and the history of Christian hostility to the Jews shows how badly that mistake can go. Paul's own teaching that 'a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly,' Romans 2:29, and his grief over his own people in Romans 9:1 to 5 set the right tone.

debates.question: What are the 'ten days' of tribulation?

views.label: A short, limited period
views.case: Ten is a round number, and Daniel 1:12 to 14 uses ten days for a brief test with a clear end. On this reading the phrase simply tells the church that its trial will be real but brief and that its length is fixed by the Lord. Many readers favour this because the letter's whole tone is one of limit and comfort.

views.label: A literal ten days
views.case: A few take the number at face value as the actual length of a coming imprisonment in Smyrna. The text does not rule it out, but nothing in the letter or in the later history of the church allows the claim to be checked.

views.label: A larger symbolic span
views.case: Some link the ten days to the ten emperors, or to a longer era of persecution. These proposals require more of the number than the context supplies, and no one agrees on whose ten days are meant.

debates.bearing: All three views keep the main point, which is that the testing has a boundary. A reader should be cautious of any view that turns the number into a calculation. What the church needed to hear was that the suffering would end and that the Lord was holding the clock.

debates.question: Who are 'those who falsely claim to be Jews'?

views.label: A local group of hostile Jews
views.case: The phrase is most naturally read as pointing to members of the city's Jewish community who slandered Christians to the authorities. 'Slander' fits an act of accusation, and the word 'synagogue' fits a gathering of such people. The charge is that they had stopped acting as the people of God while keeping the name.

views.label: A group claiming to be Jews in a wider sense
views.case: Others suggest that the phrase refers to gentiles or others who borrowed the prestige of Jewish identity, because Judaism had legal protections in the empire. The sense of 'false' is then literal: they were not who they said they were. This reading is less commonly held.

views.label: A figure for any opposition to the church
views.case: A few read the phrase as only a type of whatever group opposes God's people from inside a religious community. This takes the specific local detail out of the text.

debates.bearing: On any reading the target is a particular opposition, not a people, and the Lord's own words in Revelation 3:9 show that He expects such opponents to be brought to acknowledge His love for the church. The passage is no warrant for contempt toward Jewish people.

study.originalLanguages:
The two words for suffering in verses 9 and 10 are the same word, thlipsis, 'affliction' in the first case and 'tribulation' in the second. The church is told that the pressure it already knows will intensify, but the Lord uses one word for both, as if to say that He has been in the same trouble from the start. Thlipsis is the ordinary word for pressure and distress in the New Testament, and it is used in Revelation 7:14 for the 'great tribulation' out of which the white robed crowd has come.

The verb in 'to test you,' hina peirasthete, is peirazo, and it is worth noticing who does what. The devil throws some of them into prison, but the purpose clause names the aim as testing. The same verb is used of the devil's work in the temptation of Jesus, Matthew 4:1. The letter lets the devil act and then names a purpose beyond his own, which is the same pattern as in Job.

The imperative 'be faithful,' ginou pistos, uses the verb ginomai, which means 'become' or 'prove to be.' The tense is present, which gives the force of continuing, steady action: keep proving yourself faithful. Pistos is the adjective Christ uses of Himself in Revelation 1:5, 'the faithful witness,' and of Antipas in Revelation 2:13. The church is invited to take on the character of its Lord.

In verse 8, 'died and returned to life' translates the words egeneto nekros kai ezesen, literally 'became dead and lived.' The first verb marks a real passage into death and the second a return to life, and the pair together give the cross and resurrection in a few words.

The word for 'crown,' stephanos, was the wreath given to a victor in the games, to a public benefactor or to a person honoured at a festival. It is distinct from diadema, the royal crown of a king, which in Revelation belongs to the dragon and to Christ, Revelation 12:3 and 19:12. The faithful are therefore not promised a throne of their own; they are promised the victor's honour. The phrase 'of life' is probably appositional: the crown is life itself, as James 1:12 puts it, given to those who love the Lord.

The verb 'will not be harmed' in verse 11, ou me adikethe, uses the strong double negative of emphatic denial. It is not that the overcomer is merely unlikely to be hurt by the second death; he will certainly not be.

typology.type: The ten day test of Daniel and his friends, Daniel 1:12 to 14
typology.fulfillment: Daniel asked that he and his companions be tested for ten days on vegetables and water, and at the end they looked healthier than those who ate the king's food. The test was short, chosen in loyalty to God, and ended in vindication. Smyrna's ten days follow that shape: a brief trial of faithfulness under foreign pressure. Where Daniel could name the terms of his own test, the Smyrna church cannot, and its trial is imposed by an enemy. The correspondence is a pattern of limited testing and then vindication, not a claim that Daniel foresaw Smyrna.

typology.type: The victor's wreath, a picture of reward
typology.fulfillment: The stephanos was awarded to athletes who finished the contest, and Paul uses the image of the games for the Christian race, 1 Corinthians 9:25. In Smyrna the picture is pressed further: the athlete is asked to finish even if the race ends in death, and the prize is life itself. The earthly wreath withered and was given for one victory; the crown of life is given by the Lord and does not fade, 1 Peter 5:4. The image is not a type of one particular Old Testament thing, but it is a pattern of reward that Scripture uses of every faithful runner.

The church that is poor and rich reflects its Lord, of whom Paul says that 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. Smyrna's poverty is not a sign of divine disfavour but a share in the pattern of Christ's own descent and exaltation. The correspondence escalates in Christ, who gave up heaven's wealth for the cross; Smyrna gives up the city's goods for His sake. The type falls short where the Lord's poverty was voluntary and redemptive, and theirs, though chosen in loyalty, is not saving for anyone else.

typology.type: Death and a return to life
typology.fulfillment: The title 'who died and returned to life' is the pattern the whole letter turns on. Believers are told that they will follow the same road: dying, and then living. Paul writes that those who are united with Christ in a death like His will certainly be united with Him in a resurrection like His, Romans 6:5. For the church in Smyrna the pattern is not an abstract doctrine but a rule of life. It falls short only in that the Lord's death was a unique atonement for sin, while the believer's death is the entrance into the life Christ has already won.

study.christ:
Smyrna's letter leads to Christ more by who He is than by what He does, and each part of the introduction is doing work. He is the First and the Last, a title that in Isaiah belongs to the LORD alone, Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12. In saying it of Himself, Jesus takes the name of the God of Israel, and the church in Smyrna, which has been pressed to honour Caesar as lord, is reminded who is truly first and last. No emperor can claim the beginning or the end.

He is also the one who died and returned to life, and that is the particular comfort for those facing death. A church being asked to be faithful to death needs a Saviour who has gone through death and holds the keys. 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' He says in Revelation 1:18, and a person who holds the keys can open what others cannot. The letter's promise of safety from the second death rests on that authority. Those who are His will be harmed by the first death but not by the last.

He is the faithful witness, Revelation 1:5, who was put to death for His testimony. When He asks the church to be faithful unto death, He is not asking for something He has not given. The word martys, witness, will take on the sense of 'martyr' in later usage, and Smyrna's own history gave the word a face. The letter makes the connection that the suffering of the church is a sharing in His sufferings, as Paul says in Philippians 3:10 and Colossians 1:24.

He is the one who knows. 'I know your affliction and your poverty' is the language of a shepherd who has counted His flock. He knows poverty as well, being the one who had nowhere to lay His head, Luke 9:58, and He knows the slander of people who ought to have recognised Him, John 1:11. The Lord addresses Smyrna from experience, not from a distance.

He is the giver of the crown. The faithful receive nothing from the empire; they receive it from Him. A church that has lost its trade and its safety is promised the reward that outlasts both, and the one who promises is the Judge who will hand it out, 2 Timothy 4:8.
study.god:
This short letter shows several attributes of God with unusual clarity, and one of them is knowledge. The repeated 'I know' of the seven letters is at its most tender here. God knows the exact shape of Smyrna's trouble, and it is not generalised sympathy; He names affliction, poverty and slander. A God who knows this much is not distant, and a church that thinks itself forgotten can be corrected by the words of the Lord who has counted its losses.

He is sovereign, and the letter is careful about how. The devil is about to throw some into prison, and yet the passage never lets the devil act alone. The testing has a stated purpose, the trial has a fixed length, and the one who speaks tells His people in advance. Evil here is real and dangerous, but it is held on a leash. The same pattern is seen in Job 1:12 and in the way Jesus tells Peter that Satan has asked to sift him, Luke 22:31 to 32. Divine sovereignty does not remove the suffering; it governs it.

He is faithful to those who are faithful to Him. The reward of the crown is not a payment for services rendered but the generosity of the Lord who delights to honour those who love Him, James 1:12. A God who offers a crown to a poor congregation shows that His economy is not the city's.

He is also the Lord of life and death, and the letter holds two kinds of death together without confusing them. The first death is a real loss, and the Lord does not minimise it. The second death is the final separation from God, and from that He gives full protection to the overcomer. Here God's justice and mercy meet: the justice that will judge the world and the mercy that shelters His own from it.

For worship, the letter teaches the church to bring its fear to the one who has the right to say 'Do not fear.' It also invites the congregation to praise a God who counts poor people rich. A church that has learned from Smyrna will sing of a Lord who is worth more than the whole of a rich city, and it will not be ashamed of its own small size.

crossReferences.note: The vision of the risen Christ on which the letter's title rests. Jesus tells John not to be afraid because He is the First and the Last, the Living One who was dead and is alive forever. The words to Smyrna are the same words applied to a congregation. The comfort that quieted John is offered to a church facing prison.

A ten day test that ended in vindication for the faithful. The shape fits Smyrna's trial: short, bounded, and followed by the Lord's approval. It does not prove that Smyrna's trial will last ten literal days, but it explains why the number would have sounded like a limit rather than a threat.

The same phrase, the crown of life, promised to those who persevere under trial and love God. James states the principle that Revelation applies to a church in crisis: testing, standing the test, and the crown that God has promised. The two writers draw on a shared teaching of the early church.

Paul, near the end of his life, looks forward to the crown of righteousness awarded by the righteous Judge. The crown is not only for him but for all who long for the Lord's appearing. It places Smyrna's promise in a wider pattern of final reward given by the Lord and not earned by a performance.

Paul's definition of a true Jew as one who is circumcised in heart, by the Spirit. It explains how the Lord can speak of people who claim to be Jews and are not, without any denial of Jewish identity. The measure is faithfulness to God, and the letter to Smyrna uses that measure.

The only other mention of the synagogue of Satan, in the letter to Philadelphia, the other church that receives no rebuke. There the Lord promises that opponents will come and bow at the church's feet and know that He loves it. Smyrna's letter should be read with this promise in mind.

Those who share in the first resurrection are promised that the second death has no power over them. This is the fuller form of Smyrna's promise in verse 11. A church told that death cannot harm it is shown, later in the book, what that safety looks like when the story is complete.

The second death is identified as the lake of fire, the end of the cowardly, the faithless and the liars. The list sets Smyrna's call not to fear and to be faithful in sharp relief. The fearful and faithless are warned, and the faithful are promised that they will not share that end.

Laodicea says it is rich and is in fact wretched and poor, while Smyrna is poor and rich. The Lord offers Laodicea gold refined by fire and white garments, which Smyrna already has in the faithfulness that costs it everything. The two letters, read together, teach the church to judge its wealth by the Lord's measure.

Paul describes the apostles as poor yet making many rich, and as having nothing yet possessing everything. The same paradox that the Lord pronounces over Smyrna becomes the ordinary experience of the apostles. The poverty of a faithful church is a form of apostolic life, and its riches are shared with others.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture begins with a world made good and a man and woman crowned with glory and honour, Psalm 8:5. The fall breaks that crowning, and from then on the Bible's account of human beings is one of people who are meant for glory and find themselves in thorns. Smyrna sits at a late point in that story, and it answers the old question of what becomes of faithful people under the power of death.

The pattern of Israel's own history is the pattern that Smyrna now lives: a people in a foreign city, pressed to bow to another god, and tested for a time. Daniel's friends faced a furnace and were delivered, Daniel 3, and Daniel himself faced a den. The prophets told a persecuted people that their God was above the kings who oppressed them, and Revelation is the final form of that message to a church scattered in the empire.

The letter is also an answer to the serpent's old promise that death is not what God said it would be. Death is real, and Smyrna is told so, but it is not final. The Lord who died and came to life has taken the sting from it, and in Him the church is given a hope that the first Adam's descendants did not have. The crown of life is what was lost at the tree of life in Genesis 3:24, returned by the Lamb.

The story ends where Smyrna's promise points. In the new creation the second death is gone, and 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4. The faithful of Smyrna, whose city has long since passed, will see the crown given, and the city of God, the new Jerusalem, will have no temple to Roma and no throne of Caesar. The congregation that was poor in a rich city will find itself in a city whose streets are gold, Revelation 21:21, and it will know it was rich all along.

sermon.title: Revelation (Part 4)
sermon.why: Carson works directly through Revelation 2:8-11, drawing out how Christ meets a poor, persecuted church with comfort rather than complaint, and what the crown of life and safety from the second death mean for suffering believers.

quiz.q: How does Christ describe himself to the church in Smyrna?

options.text: The First and the Last, who died and returned to life.
options.note: Verse 8 gives this exact self-description, echoing chapter 1's vision.

options.text: The one who holds the sharp double-edged sword.
options.note: That title belongs to the letter to Pergamum, not Smyrna.

options.text: A distant judge with no personal experience of suffering.
options.note: The opposite; he identifies himself as one who has himself died and lives again.

options.text: He gives no self-description at all in this letter.
options.note: Verse 8 opens with a clear self-description drawn from chapter 1.

quiz.q: What does Christ say about Smyrna's poverty?

options.text: He knows their real poverty, yet declares that they are rich.
options.note: Verse 9 states this direct paradox.

options.text: He rebukes them for their poverty as a sign of unfaithfulness.
options.note: There is no rebuke in this letter at all; poverty is acknowledged, not blamed.

options.text: He promises to make them wealthy in earthly terms immediately.
options.note: The riches in view are spiritual, not a promise of immediate material wealth.

options.text: He says nothing about their material condition.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly addresses their affliction and poverty.

quiz.q: What does Christ tell Smyrna to expect, and how does he tell them to respond?

options.text: Some will be imprisoned and tested for ten days; they are to be faithful even unto death.
options.note: Verse 10 gives this exact warning and instruction.

options.text: He promises they will avoid all suffering entirely.
options.note: The opposite; real suffering is foretold, met with a call to fearless faithfulness.

options.text: He tells them to flee the city immediately.
options.note: The instruction is to remain faithful through the trial, not to flee.

options.text: He gives no instruction for how to respond.
options.note: He directly instructs, 'Do not fear... be faithful even unto death.'

quiz.q: What is promised to the one who overcomes in this letter?

options.text: The crown of life, and safety from the second death.
options.note: Verses 10-11 give both promises explicitly.

options.text: Immediate release from Roman imprisonment.
options.note: The promise is eternal reward, not a guarantee of immediate earthly release.

options.text: Wealth and status within the city of Smyrna.
options.note: The reward is the crown of life and safety from the second death, not earthly wealth.

options.text: No promise is given, only warning.
options.note: A specific, twofold promise closes the letter.

quiz.q: What is the 'second death' from which overcomers are promised safety?

options.text: Final, eternal separation from God after judgment, described later as the lake of fire.
options.note: Revelation 20:14 and 21:8 identify the second death this way.

options.text: Physical death, which believers are promised to avoid entirely.
options.note: Physical death is not ruled out here; some are told they will suffer even unto death.

options.text: A second occurrence of the plagues of Egypt.
options.note: The second death is a term unique to Revelation for final judgment, unrelated to the Exodus plagues.

options.text: A minor, temporary setback with no lasting significance.
options.note: It names the gravest possible outcome, eternal separation from God, from which overcomers are kept safe.

questions: Christ says he 'knows' Smyrna's affliction and poverty before he says anything else. Where do you need to remember that Christ truly knows your present hardship, not from a distance but as one who has suffered himself?
This is one of only two letters with no rebuke at all. How does it change your view of suffering to know that hardship itself is not evidence of God's displeasure?
'Do not fear what you are about to suffer' is followed immediately by a real warning of coming trial. How do you hold both the command not to fear and the reality of real difficulty together?
The trial is bounded, 'ten days,' not endless. Where in your own life do you need to trust that your present hardship has a limit set by God, even if you cannot yet see it?
The crown of life is promised to those 'faithful even unto death.' What would faithfulness look like for you this week, in whatever smaller trial you are facing?

translationNotes.note: In 'your poverty, though you are rich', the sense is an emphatic contrast between apparent and true wealth.

'Synagogue of Satan' names a specific local group hostile to the church in Smyrna; it is not a general statement about Jewish people, and should be read alongside Paul's own careful distinctions in Romans 2 and 9 about true covenant identity.
'Ten days' is widely read symbolically, following the pattern of Daniel 1:12-14, as a short, divinely bounded period rather than a literal count to be calculated toward some other event.
